text: David Eugene Tudor (January 20, 1926 – August 13, 1996) was an American pianist and composer known for his work in experimental music. He gave the first American performance of Pierre Boulez's Piano Sonata No. 2 in 1950 and later premiered works by American composers such as Morton Feldman, Earle Brown, Christian Wolff, and La Monte Young, with a particularly close association to John Cage. Cage dedicated his Klavierstück VI (1955) to Tudor, and many of Cage's compositions were written specifically for Tudor or with him in mind, as Cage stated, "what you had to do was to make a situation that would interest him." Tudor performed in the premiere of Cage's Concert For Piano and Orchestra and contributed to several recordings of Cage's music, including the Mainstream record of Cartridge Music, the Columbia Records recording of Variations II, and the two Everest records of Variations IV. He taught at the Darmstädter Ferienkurse from 1956 to 1961 and gradually shifted from performing to composing, focusing on electronic works, many commissioned for the Merce Cunningham Dance Company. His homemade musical circuits are recognized as significant contributions to live electronic music and electrical instrument building. Notable compositions include Reunion (1968), a piece co-written with Lowell Cross that features a chess game where each move triggers a lighting effect or projection, premiered with John Cage and Marcel Duchamp; and Rain Forest, a sound installation made from a metal barrel, vintage computer disk, and plastic tubing. In 1969, Tudor established India's first electronic music studio at the National Institute of Design in Ahmedabad. After John Cage's death in 1992, Tudor succeeded him as music director of the Merce Cunningham Dance Company and received the Foundation for Contemporary Arts John Cage Award in 1992. He composed Soundings: Ocean Diary (1994), the electronic component of Ocean, conceived by Cage and Cunningham, with choreography by Cunningham, orchestral music by Andrew Culver, and design by Marsha Skinner. From 1951 until the late 1960s, Tudor regularly performed Cage's indeterminate works, including Winter Music (1957), which consists of twenty pages with cluster-chords ranging from one to 61 per page, with the performer selecting which to play. Tudor consistently realized these scores, fixing his interpretations so that each performance was identical, a practice described as "pinning them down like butterflies," and used the same version in all recordings. Despite this significant role, Tudor never considered himself a composer or co-composer of the music he performed. However, Benjamin Piekut argues for distributed authorship, suggesting that the conception and sound-world of Cage's works are shared between Cage and Tudor, aligning with Cage's Buddhist anti-ego worldview. Tudor also composed the 1983 video installation Sea Tails with video artist Molly Davies and artist Jackie Matisse, in which Matisse created four kites, Davies filmed them being flown underwater near Nassau, Bahamas, for eight days, and Tudor recorded sounds both above and below deck, later layering and re-recording them onto three tapes. The installation was first presented at the Pompidou Center in 1983 and later exhibited at the Getty Center in 2004. Tudor died after a series of strokes in Tomkins Cove, New York, at the age of 70.
